## Passages to take up

Your open passages, from your journal handoff (notes/journal.md), quoted as you wrote them:

> Open passages:
> - A fresh look at the whole canvas and a detail crop in normal color, with no marks; if nothing calls, the painting is finished.

The critic's notes from its last visit (notes/critic.md), quoted as the critic wrote them. You decide what to take from them.

> From the critic's visit at the end of a sitting:
>
> Short answer: it's finished. I'd put no more marks on it.
>
> **The whole canvas.** I looked in normal color, value, squint, mirror, gallery light and relief. The picture holds at every size. There are three darks: the hull, the lead and the foreground band. Everything else sits in a high, cold key, and the apex is the hardest edge against the deepest sky. In squint the design comes down to a few shapes: the blade, the dark wedge of the hull with its two spars, the dark diagonal of the lead running into the base, and the shadow band along the bottom. In mirror it still balances, so the design doesn't depend on which way the eye reads it. The lit shard crossing the hull's side now looks like it's breaking the ship. That carries the story better than anything we talked about in earlier visits.
>
> **The four shapes from last time all landed:**
> - The left far bank (day 82) is dry and opaque. None of the old strata or lip shows through. The light on the bank starts where the sun reaches the plain.
> - T reads as the end of a plate, not a dome.
> - The wedge reads as a small lit top above a straight shadow cut.
> - The left foot no longer reads as a curb.
>
> **Places I looked hard at and would leave:**
> - **Mast foot.** At full detail a thin pale line wraps the foot of the mast and the rail. Up close you could call it drawn. At any normal viewing distance it reads as snow on a buried gunwale.
> - **The upright shard, lower left.** It's the brightest note in that quarter of the canvas. If anything still bothered me, it would be this. But it works as the full stop at the wide end of the lead, and it echoes the apex. Toning it down would mean a local patch over dry paint, and your own journal shows what those do: ghosts and tubes.
> - **The floes at the narrow end.** They still lean slightly toward a dotted line. They also describe the perspective of the lead. Acceptable.
> - **The right talus.** The bank and the drifts break it up enough. It reads as rubble now, not a row.
> - **The long shadow edge across the foreground.** It's straight and runs parallel to the horizon. As a repoussoir that's right: it frames the lit plain, and the edge of the foreground slab rising to the right keeps it from becoming a second horizon.
> - **Edges.** The even crispness is this painting's manner. Softening it now would mean painting a different picture, not finishing this one.
>
> **Why stop here.** From here on, every mark costs more than it gives. The paint is dry, and your notes show that local restatements over dry paint leave seams, rods or ghosts. Nothing I see is a fault big enough to justify that risk. The things I listed are choices, and they're consistent ones.
>
> No passage to take up first. Call it finished.

You're back at the easel. The painting is as you left it. Your brief is in BRIEF.md and your journal in notes/journal.md. Read your journal handoff and apply its practical lessons before acting. Take up your open passages: look at each in an appropriate detail crop in normal color, then improve it or accept it as it is, and say which in your journal, with your reason. A passage you've resolved or accepted comes off the list. You may finish with imperfections you deliberately accept. A fresh look at the whole canvas and detail crops in normal color can show passages the list doesn't have yet; add them to it. Continue one campaign at a time, inspecting the whole picture and relevant detail before writing the next campaign's code. Let the result inform your next action and check local repairs against the whole picture; reconsider the composition or method if a repair repeats the problem. Judge unfamiliar mixtures and marks through small laid trials on the intended substrate after the intended treatment. Carry forward the observed material conditions and treat broader rules as hypotheses. Before retrying a failed recipe, identify what has changed and why that could address the observed failure. Record what you observed and what remains uncertain. You can keep working for hours if you like, and the painting's simulated time is yours to use, whether that means days or years. Enjoy it. At the end of the sitting, record an updated handoff in your journal and last reply: the `Open passages:` list as it now stands (`Open passages: none` when nothing is open) and the practical lessons that still apply. The painting is finished when you end a sitting in which you made no marks on the painting and looked at the whole canvas and at a detail crop in normal color, even if the list still names passages. Record your reflections in your journal before you end that sitting.

Your previous sitting's reply:
I've stopped for this sitting at painting day 88. The painting is still **The Ice Keeps Her**: a brig's hull, nose up, crushed into a jagged pyramid of pack ice under a cold, deep sky. The low sun comes from the left, a dark lead of open water runs into the base of the pile, and the shadowed snow in the foreground steps down to the frame. It isn't finished yet, because I made marks this sitting.

**What I did, in the critic's order:**
- **The wedge on the big slab, bottom right:** it was a pale path leading the eye out of the bottom of the picture. Now only its squared top catches the sun, above one straight slanting shadow line. The rest is in shadow down to the frame, so it no longer pulls the eye out.
- **The rounded foot at the far left of the ice:** it read as an igloo. It's now the end of a tilted slab, with a straight top and a short step. The light dies out along the top, and the foot of the face is warmed. I painted the sky back over the old curve.
- **The small plates along the left foot:** two of them sat in a row at one height like a curb. They are now sunk under a drift.
- **The lead's far bank:** it read as a canal kerb. Two first fixes:
  - I painted a gap where the shadowed snow comes straight down to the water. My first try used the lit-snow colour, which was wrong there because that stretch is in shadow; it showed as a bright tile. A rag wouldn't lift the fresh paint off the dry layer beneath, so I painted it over in the shadow colours.
  - I made one taller stretch of wall.
- **The rest of the bank, from the left frame:** after these changes, the critic pointed out that this stretch still looked sunlit, sitting right under the shadow. I repainted it as one opaque face in the shadow colours. Now the sunlight on the bank begins where the sun actually reaches the plain, and the bottom-left corner is quiet. Once it dried, none of the old lines showed through.

**Accepted as they are:** I'm keeping the even crispness of the edges as the picture's manner. My two attempts to soften edges over dry paint both made pale rods, and the critic agrees. I'm also leaving the right-hand row of rubble at the base, the small upright shard in the near left, the sunk near plate, and a hairline at the left frame along the water's edge.

**Open passages:**
- One fresh look at the whole canvas and a detail crop, with no marks. If nothing calls for work, the painting is finished.

**Lessons that still apply:**
- Repaint big faces in one broad pass and smooth it once along the slope. Opaque full coverage hides old lines; small patches leave ghosts.
- Check the value of the spot before painting snow there: anything in a shadow zone needs the shadow colours.
- New paint over dry paint won't fully wipe off; paint over it instead.
- Don't smooth a band across a dry edge (it becomes a rod). A single straight shadow cut works.
- Rounded ends with an even light rim read as domes or trays. Straight runs, a step, and light that dies out read as ice.

## BRIEF.md

# Paint a picture

Compose and paint one original picture in the manner of Caspar David
Friedrich, at the easel, a simulator of oil paint on linen. His pictures
are composed in large, simple masses, and over those masses they carry a
great deal of particular detail, each small form drawn and painted on its
own. The place, subject and composition are yours to invent. Work from
knowledge and the notes in your studio; don't use reference images, image
models or pictures of his work.

## Your studio
- The folder [local path redacted] this brief, your notes and the easel.
- The easel's tools are `paint`, `look`, `note`, `status` and `log`;
  notes/easel_guide.md explains them.
- There is no undo. To change a passage, paint over it, or lift wet
  paint with a rag or a brush.
- You mix your own paint on the palette, from the tubes, in the
  proportions you choose.
- Time passes on the painting's own clock: every mark takes the time a
  hand takes, and `wait(minutes)` lets it rest, as long as you like; paint
  dries as that time passes. Real time between chunks doesn't count.

## The rules of the studio
- Paint shapes and marks, not computed pictures: don't encode an image in
  masks, amounts or proportions.
- Shapes are drawn, not copied: don't make a mask or stroke by mirroring
  or rotating another mask's or stroke's coordinates. A shape that mirrors
  another is drawn as its own shape, not as `m:at(x, 2*H - y)` or
  `m:at(W - x, y)`. Moving a shape and reusing your own helpers are fine.

## What to read
notes/easel_guide.md; notes/techniques.md; notes/studio_notes.md;
notes/research/friedrich_materials.md (his materials and method, sourced) and
notes/research/oil_paint_physics.md as needed.

After choosing a subject or technical question, use `reference` to search
the studio's reference library, or `reference_list` to browse its titles.
Read a result with `reference` by its id; follow next_page
until it is null to read the full text.

Another painter visits your studio as a critic, at the end of each sitting
and whenever you ask for a visit with `ask_critic`. The critic looks at the
painting with the same `look` you use and reads your journal and the note
you give `ask_critic` (kept in notes/to_critic.md); it doesn't paint. It
writes what it would fix and why in notes/critic.md, which you get at the
start of your next sitting or as `ask_critic`'s reply.

## Choosing the picture
Before you paint, write eight different pictures you could make from this brief in notes/concepts.md, numbered 1 to 8, each in a sentence or two. After each one, write your estimate of how many painters out of a hundred given this brief would make that picture. The studio sets aside the two with the highest estimates, rolls a die among the other six and tells you which one is yours. You make every decision from there, and the picture can develop wherever the painting takes it.

## Working
Work one campaign at a time. After laying a campaign, inspect the whole picture in normal color and relevant detail before writing the code for the next campaign. Let what you see inform the next action; record what changes or why continuing unchanged serves the picture.

After the first large masses, consider whether the whole picture produces your intended effect: how its large shapes, values and spatial relationships support it, and whether anything weakens it. Improve a weakening relationship in the large masses, or deliberately accept it with your reason, before you build detail over them. After a local repair, check its effect on the whole picture. If the repair recreates the problem, reconsider the composition or method before expanding it.

Before repeating an unfamiliar mixture or stroke, inspect a small trial, on the scratch canvas beside the painting (`scratch: true`) or on the painting, laid on the intended substrate after the intended treatment, alongside the existing marks in a detail crop. A held pile shows thick paint on steel; use the laid trial to judge its effect on the picture. For material trials and repairs, keep useful observations in your journal: substrate and wetness, recipe ratios, medium or thinner, brush load, coverage and the viewed result. Carry forward the conditions that mattered and label broader rules as hypotheses until a further trial isolates them.

- You make every artistic decision.
- Keep exploring what interests you. You’re free to reconsider a passage,
  change approach and discover where the painting can go.
- Keep a working journal with `note` as you go: your own working notes.
  You can revise them.
- You may sign the painting.
- Take your time and enjoy painting. You can keep working for hours,
  exploring and revisiting passages.
- An oil painting can develop over simulated years. Whether yours takes
  one simulated day or a thousand, that time is yours to use.
- Your journal handoff at the end of each sitting lists the passages
  still open under a line reading `Open passages:`, or reads
  `Open passages: none` when nothing is open, and the next sitting opens
  with that list. The painting is finished when you end a sitting in
  which you made no marks on the painting and looked at the whole canvas
  and at a detail crop in normal color, even if the list still names
  passages. Record your reflections in your journal before you end that
  sitting.

## Your reply
When you stop working, reply with the painting's title if you give it one
and a few sentences about the picture.

## Your journal (notes/journal.md)

Your own notes, quoted as you wrote them:

> - day 1, 09:00: ## Sitting 1 — plan
>   Concept 6: a ship's hull caught and half buried in a jagged pyramid of pack ice, cold blue Arctic sky.
>   My own arrangement (not the Eismeer's): canvas 1050 mm, aspect 1.4 (W1000 x H714), linen 15/13, warm ground: knife layer white2/red earth1/ochre1 90µm, brushed top layer white8/ochre0.25/umber0.08 45µm (patchy, pinkish showing).
>   Composition: horizon y=440. Pyramid apex ~(630,90), base ~250..950; low sun from the LEFT: left/upward faces lit warm, right flank in cool shadow, pyramid casts shadow right across the plain. Ship's bow (brig) thrust up-left out of the left shoulder at ~25°, bowsprit pointing into the empty left; mast stump leaning right across a lit slab. Dark lead of open water in left foreground narrowing to the pyramid base; large lit tilted slab bottom right; low distant bergs on horizon; a low mid-distance ridge at left.
>   Studies on scratch (scratch-2, -3): lit ice vanished against a pale sky -> sky top must be deeper (~value 130-150) for the apex to read; the hull read as a fin until bowsprit + mast were added; the hull looked flying because no ice under/in front of it -> add slabs under the bow and one slab tip crossing in front of the hull side, extend the base left to ~250.
> - day 3, 16:19: ## Lay-in (day 1–3)

I've stopped, and **The Ice Keeps Her** is finished. I made no marks in this sitting. I looked at the whole canvas in normal color and at three close-ups: the hull where it meets the ice, the lead and the near-left corner, and the right base. Nothing needed more work.

The picture shows a brig's hull caught nose up in a jagged pyramid of pack ice. A low sun comes from the left under a deep, cold sky. The apex is the hardest edge, set against the darkest part of the sky. There are only three darks: the hull, the dark lead of open water running into the base of the pile, and the shadowed snow along the bottom. Everything else stays high, pale and cold. A lit slab of ice crosses the hull's side, so the ship looks broken by the ice rather than just sitting on it.

There are a few small flaws I've chosen to keep:
- **The snow bank on the right:** at its foot it's a little soft next to the crisp plates around it.
- **The floating ice:** the floes in the narrow end of the lead still sit a bit like a dotted line.
- **The mast foot:** a thin pale line wraps it.
- **The edges:** they're crisp everywhere. Friedrich would let some fade out, but my two attempts to soften edges over dry paint left pale bands.

All the paint is dry now, and on this painting small patches over dry paint have always left visible marks. Fixing any of these would risk more than it gains.

The main lesson, now in the journal: decide which edges to soften while the paint is still wet, in the first layer, not at the end.

Open passages: none

Lessons that still apply:
- Repaint big faces whole, in one broad pass with one blend along the slope. Small patches over dry lines leave faint marks.
- Check the value of a spot before painting snow there. Anything in shadow needs the shadow colours.
- New paint over dry paint won't fully wipe off. Paint over it instead.
- Don't blend a band across a dry edge, because it turns into a pale rod. Soften edges in the wet first layer.
- Rounded ends with an even light rim look like domes or trays. Straight runs, a step and light that fades out look like ice.
